threat_assessment: The table will misread you twice, and both misreads are yours to manage. Early on, Howling Mine, Temple Bell, and Kami of the Crescent Moon read as group hug — everyone's drawing, nobody's dying, and forced-draw decks get parked in the 'hug until it isn't' bin. Let them. Threat deflection is managing your perceived threat below your actual one (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), and a deck whose verified kill pieces are a one-mana Iron Maiden and a two-mana Ebony Owl Netsuke is built to be underestimated. But know the counter-read: this list carries eight Game Changers (bracket floor 4 — bracket_report), and a turn-one Rhystic Study or Mystic Remora tells every experienced pilot at the table what bracket you're actually playing. Some tables will also 'know' you as the Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring infinite deck — that pairing has 296k combo-DB popularity — when stack 001 refuted it for this deck: with only those two cards, no repeatable sequence exists. The real engine is three cards (stack 004: Sol Ring plus Arcane Signet or Thought Vessel, exactly mana-neutral per cycle) and it nets nothing on its own; the Aetherflux Reservoir exit is unverified and stays a 'needs a stack scenario' until proven. You can quietly correct that misread to buy peace, or let it stand when you want removal pointed at a threat you don't actually have — judgment call, but make it consciously. What actually threatens you is narrow and specific. First, artifact and enchantment sweepers: your draw engines, all three punishers, nine mana rocks, Propaganda, and Ghostly Prison sit in one blast radius, while creature wraths hit almost nothing you care about — so deploy the engine in layers, keep Loran and countermagic for the Farewell-class spell, and remember Teferi's Protection phases out your whole board, not just your life total. Second, your own symmetry: every Mine effect is real cards in a combo or storm player's hand, and the strategy corpus has no school that blesses donating resources — treat that as the live risk it is. The flip from hug to kill has a number attached: the core two-piece (engine + punisher) is assembled by turn 6 in only 34.3% of goldfish runs, 49.1% ever. So most games you are a draw-go control deck holding interaction (held in 73.4% of runs) while Heliod lands on schedule (mean 4.125, 90.5% by turn 6) and makes everything flash. When the two-piece does land, embrace archenemy openly: stack 003 verifies 7 damage on the punished upkeep — and the cleanup step trims their hand back to exactly 7, so the clock reloads itself every rotation without you tapping out. A clock that runs during everyone else's draw step is inevitability (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock); once it's live, your only job is protecting it. The other flip is quieter: Mystical Tutor at your last opponent's end step with seven-plus mana implied is the loudest tell in the deck — per stack 002, the second Approach of the Second Sun wins on resolution and the table's only window is countering that second cast. Commit inside the window where they can't profitably answer (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window): count their open mana, hold Dovin's Veto or Swan Song for the commit turn, and don't telegraph a turn early.
matchups: Against aggro, you're the control deck and happy about it (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Propaganda and Ghostly Prison are virtual card advantage tripled — one enchantment taxes three players' attack steps (strategy:card-advantage.virtual) — and the punishers turn defense into a clock their damage-per-card can't beat (strategy:life-as-resource.philosophy-of-fire). The trap is sequencing: Forced Fruition into an empty aggro hand is a full refill of live threats. Punishers before or with the big draw pieces, so the refill arrives pre-taxed (strategy:critical-mass) — and save Path and Swords for the one commander that ignores fort taxes. Against spellslinger and storm, be honest with yourself: your engine is their engine. Forced Fruition hands a storm pilot seven cards per spell — against those pods it is a liability, and holding it is a real line, not cowardice. Deploy the asymmetric layer (Rhystic Study, Remora, Smothering Tithe — Remora against a spell-dense pod is one of the best cards in your 99) and bank the free suite for the enabler that ends the game, per the answer-economy bar (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy): counter the ritual engine or the payoff, never the cantrip. Goldfish says you're holding free or cheap interaction in 73.4% of games — that's your matchup plan in one number. In control mirrors, someone must be the beatdown and it isn't you: Iron Maiden and Ebony Owl advance through every draw-go turn, so inevitability is yours and you can let them act first (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Heliod's back face makes your whole deck flash-speed and discounts it per opponent draw — you literally never have to tap out on your own turn. Hullbreaker Horror is the mirror-breaker: flash, can't be countered, and every cheap spell you cast afterward bounces their permanent or their spell — a counter-war where your Swan Song also Boomerangs their threat is a war you win. When you go for Approach, stack 002 is your script: the win is checked when the second cast resolves, and their one window is that cast — so commit only with Dovin's Veto (uncounterable by their blue) or Fierce Guardianship in hand, and count every blue mana at the table first. Against combo and graveyard decks, your interaction is your hate — the deck runs no dedicated graveyard pieces, so the plan is 002's framing turned around: every deck that wins 'on resolution' has one interaction window exactly like your Approach does, and your job is knowing theirs as precisely as you know yours. Free countermagic on the enabler, Swords on the reanimated body, Cyclonic Rift as the reset button when the window's already passed. Two judgment flags: your forced draws fill delve- and escape-style graveyards as a side effect — against those decks the Mine effects cost more than they look — and Homeward Path is a silver bullet against Agent-of-Treachery-style theft decks worth fetching with your utility-land count. Above all, respect your own consistency math: two-piece by turn 6 in 34.3% of games means you sculpt, you do not race. Mulligan engine-half hands that can dig, ship punisher-only hands (strategy:mulligans.engine-hands), and win the long game you were built to own.
how_it_wins:
This deck hands the whole table a firehose of cards, then charges for the water. The engines — Howling Mine, Font of Mythos, Temple Bell, Dictate of Kruphix, Kami of the Crescent Moon, Folio of Fancies, and above all Forced Fruition — are perfectly symmetric on their face. The punishers make them anything but: Iron Maiden and Viseling deal upkeep damage equal to hand size minus 4, and Ebony Owl Netsuke deals a flat 4 to anyone at seven or more cards. Stack 003 verified the arithmetic that makes this a real clock: once Forced Fruition has filled a hand, cleanup trims the opponent to exactly 7 cards, and the next upkeep Owl hits for 4 and Maiden for 3 — 7 damage, from you, without tapping a single land. Both artifacts trigger on each opponent's upkeep, so the tax runs three ways while you sit behind counterspells. That is the default win: attrition with inevitability, defended by a counter suite the goldfish sim says you're holding in 73% of games.

The clean kill is Approach of the Second Sun. The first cast gains 7 life and buries the card seventh from the top — trivially shallow in a deck where everyone draws in bulk and Teferi's Ageless Insight doubles your own draws — or Mystical Tutor and Long-Term Plans put it back on top directly. Stack 002 verified the second cast end to end: the win condition is checked during resolution, as a spell effect, and the first casting still counts because the game tracks the casting event in its history, not the card that got shuffled away. The opponents' only window is while the second Approach is on the stack. Commit on the turn you can protect it — Swan Song countering their counter was walked through explicitly — because once resolution begins, nothing stops it.

The third piece is an engine, not a win: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + a two-mana rock (stack 004). Each rock's cast triggers the Horror to bounce the other rock — a legal target, because at that moment it is a permanent — and tapping each rock before it bounces makes the cycle exactly mana-neutral: 3 spent, 3 produced, unbounded casts in a single main phase. It nets zero mana, zero cards, zero damage on its own. The flagged lethal outlet is Aetherflux Reservoir — 1 life per spell cast this turn, then Pay 50 life for 50 damage — but that four-card line has not been stack-verified; treat it as a candidate, not a fact. And know what the deck does NOT do: the combo database's two-card Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring 'infinite' is refuted (stack 001). The pair alone produces nothing.

Heliod is the hinge that makes all of it asymmetric. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; a sorcery-speed {3}{U/P} flips him into the Warped Eclipse, which grants everything flash and discounts your spells by {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn. Your own engines pay your mana bill: on a Font of Mythos board an opponent turn cycle can make your next spell nearly free, cast at instant speed, with countermagic still up. The goldfish sim has Heliod down by turn 6 in 90% of games — the deck's most reliable single event.

combo_lines.001: What this deck does NOT do. The combo database lists Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring as a two-card infinite (296,000 decks believe it); this walk refutes it. The Horror's trigger is modal, and mode and target lock in while the Sol Ring that caused it is still a spell on the stack — a spell you control is not a legal target for 'target spell you don't control,' and it is not a nonland permanent either. By the time Sol Ring is a permanent, the trigger is gone. The pair alone loops nothing: no mana, no storm count. Never pitch this deck to the table — or compute its bracket — on the strength of that database line.
combo_lines.002: The second Approach of the Second Sun, put on top by Mystical Tutor and cast from your hand. The two questions that decide games: yes, the first casting still counts even though the card was shuffled back into your library — the condition checks an event in the game's history, not the card object — and the win is checked mid-resolution, as a spell effect, not a state-based action. The opponents' one and only window is while Approach sits on the stack; the walk plays out the counter-war, including Swan Song answering their counterspell with {U} held. Once all players pass and resolution begins, the game simply ends.
combo_lines.003: The punisher core doing its job under fire. An opponent tries to Naturalize Forced Fruition — and the Fruition trigger sits on top of the very spell that caused it, so they draw their seven cards before the enchantment dies (and the ability would survive its source's destruction anyway). Cleanup trims them to exactly 7 in hand, which is precisely the threshold both punishers want: next upkeep, Ebony Owl Netsuke's intervening-if sees seven cards and deals 4, Iron Maiden deals 7 minus 4 = 3, for 7 total. Both triggers are yours, so you order them — though here neither changes hand size, so the math is order-proof.
combo_lines.004: The real Hullbreaker engine — three cards, not two. Cast the two-mana rock; the Horror's trigger targets Sol Ring, which IS a legal target because it's on the battlefield, a permanent, not a spell. Tap Sol Ring for {C}{C} while the trigger is on the stack (a mana ability — nothing can respond), let the bounce resolve, recast Sol Ring, bounce and tap the Signet in turn. One full cycle: 3 mana spent, 3 produced — exactly mana-neutral, so the cast count is unbounded within one main phase off a {2} investment. It nets no mana, cards, or damage by itself, and aiming a trigger at an opponent's permanent breaks the chain. Thought Vessel substitutes for Arcane Signet exactly; Fellwar Stone only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.

card_roles.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: Front face: a 4/4 that returns a non-God enchantment from your graveyard on arrival — Forced Fruition or Rhystic Study back after a wrath is the usual pick. The {3}{U/P} flip (sorcery speed, payable with 2 life) turns on the deck: the Warped Eclipse grants all your spells flash and discounts them {1} per card your opponents drew this turn — your own table-draw engines pay your costs while you keep mana up for counters.
card_roles.Forced Fruition: The punisher core's detonator: every opponent spell is seven forced draws, feeding Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, and Viseling past their thresholds instantly. Stack 003 verified the trigger resolves even when the spell it triggered on is the removal that kills it.
card_roles.Iron Maiden: Hand-size-minus-4 damage at each opponent's upkeep, computed on resolution. Inert against a five-card hand; a three-a-turn clock once the engines are running.
card_roles.Ebony Owl Netsuke: A flat 4 at each opponent's upkeep at seven-plus cards — the intervening-if is checked both at trigger and on resolution. With Iron Maiden, exactly 7 damage per punished upkeep off a cleanup-trimmed hand (stack 003).
card_roles.Viseling: Iron Maiden with a body — same hand-minus-4 upkeep damage on a 1/1 construct. Redundancy for the deck's core clock; dies to creature removal where the Maiden doesn't.
card_roles.Psychosis Crawler: Drains each opponent for 1 per card YOU draw, and its stats track your hand. With the X-draw suite (Mathemagics, Prosperity, Braingeyser, Stroke of Genius) it converts a big refill into table-wide reach — a candidate line flagged for stack verification, not yet walked.
card_roles.Scrawling Crawler: A symmetric upkeep draw stapled to an asymmetric tax: each opponent draw costs them a life, so every engine on your board turns it into a slow burn.
card_roles.Sphinx's Tutelage: Turns your own draws into repeated two-card mills with a shared-color cascade — an alternate attrition angle that scales with Ageless Insight and the wheels.
card_roles.Chasm Skulker: Grows with every card you draw and leaves a squid army when answered — a cheap threat that turns your engine advantage into a board without spending extra cards.
card_roles.Howling Mine: The classic symmetric engine: an extra draw at each draw step while untapped. Symmetric on its face; the punishers and Heliod's discount make it yours.
card_roles.Font of Mythos: Howling Mine doubled — two extra draws for everyone. The fastest way to push the table to seven cards, and the biggest per-turn Heliod discount.
card_roles.Temple Bell: A draw for everyone on demand, at instant speed — which means you can ring it on an opponent's upkeep after their draw step to push a hand over the punisher threshold, or in response to removal for pure value.
card_roles.Dictate of Kruphix: The flash Howling Mine — deploy it end of turn, ahead of the opponent whose upkeep you most want taxed.
card_roles.Kami of the Crescent Moon: Howling Mine on legs for two mana. Cheapest engine in the deck; also the most fragile.
card_roles.Folio of Fancies: Three jobs: removes YOUR maximum hand size, force-feeds the table X cards at once, and can mill an opponent for their whole (bloated) hand. The X-draw activation is the precision tool for pushing hands over 7 at the right moment.
card_roles.Horn of Greed: Draws on every land play — modest for opponents (one land a turn), steady for you, and another trigger keeping hands fat.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: The asymmetric half of the value layer: every opponent spell is a card or a tax, and in a deck this dense with forced action it is a firehose. The Warped Eclipse doesn't discount off it (it counts draws, and Study's draws are yours) — but it wins the card war that decides control mirrors.
card_roles.Mystic Remora: Rhystic Study's early-game twin — a turn-1 Remora often draws three-plus cards before the cumulative upkeep bites. Pay a couple of ages, then let it go.
card_roles.Smothering Tithe: Every opponent draw is {2} or a Treasure for you — and this deck makes opponents draw in sevens. Forced Fruition plus Tithe presents seven pay-or-treasure decisions per opponent spell (flagged for stack verification of the exact yield).
card_roles.Consecrated Sphinx: Two cards to you for every card an opponent draws. Under any table engine this is obscene; under Forced Fruition it is fourteen cards per opponent spell. The single strongest magnet for removal you play.
card_roles.Teferi's Ageless Insight: Doubles every draw of yours past the first each draw step — your Howling Mines become personal Fonts, and digging seven cards to a buried Approach takes half the turns.
card_roles.Faerie Mastermind: Flash body that pays you a card whenever an opponent draws their second card each turn — free value under your own engines — with an activated Temple Bell stapled on for pushing hands at instant speed.
card_roles.Hullbreaker Horror: An uncounterable flash 7/8 that bounces a spell or permanent on every cast you make — tempo monster in the mid game, and the heart of the verified three-card cast engine with Sol Ring plus any true two-mana rock (stack 004). The two-card 'infinite' with Sol Ring alone is refuted (stack 001).
card_roles.Displacer Kitten: Blinks one of your nonland permanents on each noncreature cast: reset a tapped rock, rebuy Heliod's or Loran's or Agent of Treachery's arrival trigger. Its interaction with the 004 engine is flagged as a candidate line, unverified.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The best rock in the format and one of the two battlefield pieces of the verified Hullbreaker loop — the loop taps it for {C}{C} with the bounce trigger already on the stack.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Fixes into either color and serves as the third piece of the 004 engine: its cast bounces Sol Ring, its tap keeps the cycle at exactly 3-in, 3-out.
card_roles.Thought Vessel: Two jobs verified or textual: an exact substitute for Arcane Signet in the Hullbreaker loop (same neutral ledger, per stack 004), and no-maximum-hand-size insurance for your own engine output.
card_roles.Fellwar Stone: Ramp that reads opponents' lands — and a conditional loop piece: it sustains the 004 engine only while an opponent controls a land that produces mana; on an empty board the cycle goes mana-negative and the loop dies.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: Free countermagic while Heliod is out — the card that lets you tap out for an engine piece and still say no. Part of why the sim shows interaction held in 73% of games.
card_roles.Force of Negation: The other free counter: pitch a blue card on an opponent's turn to stop a noncreature spell and exile it. Guards the punisher board through your tapped-out turns.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the counterspell aimed at your second Approach — the exact play walked in stack 002. The 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One-mana noncreature counter; the two Treasures you hand over are a real cost, so aim it at spells that matter — sweepers, counters in the Approach war.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The argument-ender: can't be countered itself. The premium hold for your commit turn.
card_roles.Counterspell: The unconditional classic. Two blue is easy in a 36-source blue base.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Counters anything for {1}{U} and replaces itself next upkeep; the two cards it feeds the opponent are, in this deck, more fuel for your punishers.
card_roles.Approach of the Second Sun: The clean wincon. First cast: 7 life and seventh from the top — shallow when everyone's drawing in bulk. Second cast from hand wins during resolution, verified end to end in stack 002; the only window to stop it is on the stack.
card_roles.Aetherflux Reservoir: Life per spell per cast, then Pay 50 life: 50 damage. The natural payoff for the 004 cast engine and for Heliod-discounted flurries — but the four-card lethal is a flagged candidate awaiting a stack scenario, not a verified line.
card_roles.White Sun's Zenith: Instant-speed X cats that shuffle back for later — a wincon that lives in your library where counterspells can't find it, deployed on the end step before your swing.
card_roles.Secure the Wastes: Instant-speed X warriors: a board out of nowhere with all your held-up mana at someone's end step, or emergency blockers.
card_roles.Monastery Mentor: Every noncreature spell — most of the deck — makes a prowess monk. Under a Heliod discount turn it converts a cheap flurry into a real board.
card_roles.Metallurgic Summonings: Constructs sized to each instant or sorcery you cast; the buyback clause returns your whole spell graveyard once you control six artifacts, which this deck reaches without trying.
card_roles.Mystical Tutor: The Approach enabler: end-step tutor puts the second copy on top for the win next turn (stack 002's setup). Also finds the right counterspell on demand.
card_roles.Long-Term Plans: Any card, third from the top — with your draw density that's one turn away, two with Ageless Insight out. Unlike Mystical Tutor it can fetch permanents: Aetherflux, a punisher, the missing loop rock.
card_roles.Mathemagics: Draws 2^X cards — the most explosive refill in the deck and the scariest thing to point at yourself with Psychosis Crawler out (candidate line, unverified).
card_roles.Prosperity: Symmetric X-draw for the table: pushes every hand toward punisher range at once, on your terms.
card_roles.Skyscribing: Prosperity with a forecast rider — a free-ish draw for everyone each upkeep from your hand, keeping hands topped up without spending the card.
card_roles.Braingeyser: Targeted X-draw: refill yourself, or force-feed one opponent over the Netsuke threshold at sorcery speed.
card_roles.Stroke of Genius: Braingeyser at instant speed — refill on an end step, or push a hand over 7 in response to their upkeep triggers going on the stack.
card_roles.Dig Through Time: Delve makes this two mana in the mid game: seven deep for exactly the two cards you need — usually a counter and a threat, or the buried Approach.
card_roles.Brass Infiniscope: A rock that pays you a card (and half-X life) on your next X-spell — a small bridge between the ramp suite and the X-draw suite.
card_roles.Ghostly Prison: Pays for the deck's low creature count: attackers cost {2} each, and the whole table's mana is already stretched by your taxes.
card_roles.Propaganda: Ghostly Prison's blue twin. Two copies of this effect plus punisher upkeep damage makes attacking you the worst-value line at the table.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The panic button: life locked, everything phases out, you lose nothing to the wrath — and your engine board returns intact before your untap.
card_roles.Cyclonic Rift: The asymmetric reset. Overloaded on an end step it clears every opposing board while your punisher artifacts stay put.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Premium one-mana creature exile; the life you give away comes back as upkeep damage.
card_roles.Path to Exile: The second one-mana exile. The basic land you gift is a real cost — save it for the creature that actually kills you.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: Artifact/enchantment removal on a body, plus a tap that draws you and an opponent a card — removal that also feeds the punishers.
card_roles.Agent of Treachery: Steal the best permanent on the table — often the thing your counterspells missed — and the Displacer Kitten rebuy is the flagged dream.
card_roles.Torrential Gearhulk: Flash 5/6 that recasts a counterspell or Dig Through Time from the graveyard for free — a threat that interacts the turn it arrives.
card_roles.United Front: X allies plus a counter on each creature you control — turns held mana into a board that grows your utility bodies.
card_roles.Leyline of Anticipation: Flash for everything before Heliod flips (and redundancy after) — free from the opening hand, which is when the deck most wants to play draw-go.
card_roles.Reliquary Tower: No maximum hand size on a land — your engines fill your hand too, and you are the one player who shouldn't discard for it.
card_roles.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: A Temple Bell on a land: repeatable, uncounterable hand-stuffing that survives every board wipe.
card_roles.Homeward Path: The Agent-of-Treachery mirror-breaker and theft insurance — everyone takes their own creatures back, which usually means you take yours back.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Haste and shroud for Heliod or Hullbreaker Horror — protecting the flip turn is its main job here.

mulligan: The sim keeps 74% of first sevens and the deck mulligans gently (0.34 per game), so the bar is: two to four lands (the kept-hand distribution centers on 2–3 plus rocks — 18 lands means the nine rocks are load-bearing, and Ancient Tomb plus a two-drop rock is how 27% of games cast Heliod by turn 3), one card-flow piece, and something to say 'no' with. What you are actually mulliganing toward is flow plus interaction, not the combo: a table engine or an asymmetric engine (Rhystic Study, Mystic Remora, Ageless Insight) arrives by turn 6 in 62% and 49% of games respectively, and cheap or free interaction is in hand 73% of the time — those are the reliable axes. The full two-piece — engine PLUS punisher — is assembled by turn 6 in only 34% of games, so never keep a marginal hand because it 'promises the lock'; the punishers are inert on their own (Iron Maiden reads hand minus 4 — against a normal hand that's one damage). Conversely, a hand of two punishers and no draw engine is a mulligan in costume. Ship it. Don't mulligan chasing Approach either: win-condition access shows up in 61% of games on its own, and Mystical Tutor or Long-Term Plans finds it when the board is ready. Heliod himself needs no help — 90% of games cast him by turn 6, median turn 4 — so keep hands that use the turns before him: Remora into rock into Kami is the curve the deck was built to play.
upgrades: The obsolescence index has real entries for this list's mana, and one clear target: Worn Powerstone. It's flagged as superseded by the two-mana Talisman class at lower cost — and the deck already owns the in-identity copies (Talisman of Progress, the Signets), so the actionable reading is that Powerstone is your first cut when trimming: it enters tapped, costs three, and note that stack 004's loop math also excludes it as an engine rock (the loop needs a castable two-drop that taps immediately). Azorius Signet's entry lists Mind Stone among its superseders — 'additional: draw' — a fair swap only if you value the late-game cash-in over colored fixing in a two-color deck; the index also flags Fellwar Stone as obsoleted by Sol Ring on cost, but you already run Sol Ring, and Fellwar's real demerit here is the verified one: it only sustains the Hullbreaker loop while an opponent's land can make mana. Long-Term Plans is indexed as obsoleted by Mystical Tutor, which you also already run — but the index's supersession is narrower than it looks, since Plans fetches any card (a punisher, Aetherflux) where Mystical only finds instants and sorceries; keep both unless you need the slot. Counterspell draws index entries for Syncopate and Spell Snare on cost alone — both are conditional counters by their own text, a poor trade in a deck that plans to hold mana anyway; note it and move on. Brass Infiniscope is flagged for Daily Bugle Newspaper (cheaper, with token/discard riders) — worth the swap if the X-spell rider rarely fires for you. And the important negative result: the punisher core itself — Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, Viseling, Howling Mine, Font of Mythos — has no obsolescence entries at all. Nothing printed since does this job better; the old cards are the tech, not the debt.
